## Today we cover

::: {.incremental}
- **electrophoresis** — agarose, polyacrylamide, DGGE, Southern blotting;
- **allozymes** — the first molecular markers, and why they lost;
- **PCR** — what it needs, melting temperature, qPCR, RT-qPCR, ddPCR;
- **Sanger sequencing** — terminators, capillaries, reading a gel;
- **fragment length polymorphisms** — RFLP, AFLP, RAPD, microsatellites, ISSR.
:::

::: {.notes}
The through-line: every method here separates molecules by size or by charge, and reads the pattern. Once you see that, the differences are details of chemistry.
:::

# Electrophoresis

## Electrophoresis principle

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Gel electrophoresis is a simple, rapid, and sensitive analytical technique for separating **charged particles**.
- Gels are porous; the size of the pores relative to the molecule determines whether — and how easily — it passes.
- Separation therefore depends on **charge, size, and shape**.
- Most biomolecules carry a net charge at any pH other than their **isoelectric point**.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p03_2.jpg)
:::
:::

## Two gel materials, two apparatus types

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p04_2.jpg){height="250px"}

**Horizontal (submarine)** — agarose, run under buffer; the standard for nucleic acids.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p04_3.jpg){height="250px"}

**Vertical** — polyacrylamide, used mostly for proteins and for high-resolution sizing.
:::
:::

## Agarose electrophoresis

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- Agarose is a natural colloid isolated from **seaweed** — a linear polysaccharide of repeating agarobiose units (alternating 3,6-anhydrogalactose and galactose).
- Larger pore size, so it suits molecules **above ~200 kDa**.
- Used for both proteins and nucleic acids.
- Typical working concentration: **1–3%**.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p05_2.jpg)

Longer molecules stay near the well; shorter ones run further towards the anode.
:::
:::

## Seeing the DNA — gel dyes

DNA dyes are what make the separation visible, during or after the run. They differ in **sensitivity**, **toxicity**, and **compatible detection** (UV or blue light).

| Dye | Notes |
|---|---|
| Ethidium bromide (EtBr) | classic, very sensitive, intercalating — mutagenic, UV |
| SYBR Green | high sensitivity, blue-light compatible |
| GelGreen | designed as a safer EtBr replacement |
| SYBR Safe | blue light, lower toxicity, routine teaching-lab choice |
| Methylene blue | insensitive but non-toxic and visible in daylight |

::: {.callout-warning}
"Safer" is not "safe". Every intercalating dye binds DNA — including yours.
:::

## Polyacrylamide gels

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Chains of **acrylamide** monomers cross-linked with **bisacrylamide** (N,N′-methylenebisacrylamide).
- Pore size and resolving power depend entirely on the acrylamide : bisacrylamide concentration — normally **5–25%**.
- Separates proteins of **5–250 kDa** and polynucleotides from **<5 to ~3000 bp**.
- **SDS-PAGE** coats proteins with a uniform negative charge, so they separate by **mass alone**.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p07_2.jpg)
:::
:::

## Denaturing gradient gel electrophoresis (DGGE)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p06_2.jpg){height="380px"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
Polyacrylamide gels containing a **gradient of chemical denaturants** — urea and formamide.

Fragments of identical length but different sequence melt at different positions in the gradient and stop migrating there. A **GC-rich clamp** on one primer keeps the fragment from melting completely.

![](/assets/lecture2/p06_3.jpg){height="140px"}
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
DGGE was the community-fingerprinting workhorse before amplicon sequencing — one band, roughly one sequence type.
:::

## Southern blotting

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- An RFLP method that involves **no PCR amplification**.
- Developed by **Edward M. Southern (1975)**.
- DNA fragments are separated by electrophoresis, transferred to a **nylon membrane**, and identified by **labelled probe hybridisation**.
- The probe is complementary to the target and carries a marker for detection.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p08_2.jpg)
:::
:::

## Codominant vs dominant markers

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p09_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Codominant** markers (a) discriminate homozygotes from heterozygotes — you see both alleles.

**Dominant** markers (b) do not: presence of a band means "at least one copy", so *AA* and *Aa* are indistinguishable.

::: {.callout-important}
This single property decides which population-genetic statistics you are allowed to calculate.
:::
:::
:::

# Allozymes

## The allozyme era

**Allozymes** — proteins differing in electrophoretic mobility as a result of allelic differences in the protein sequence, which ultimately reflect variation in the corresponding DNA sequence.

Population genetics entered the molecular age with two 1966 papers describing electrophoretically detectable variation in:

i. *Drosophila pseudoobscura* — **Lewontin and Hubby 1966**;
ii. humans — **Harris 1966**.

Genetic diversity was measured in two ways:

i. the average proportion of loci **heterozygous in an individual** — heterozygosity or gene diversity, **H**;
ii. the average proportion of loci **polymorphic in the population** — gene polymorphism, **P**.

## Allozymes and isozymes

::: {.incremental}
- **Allozymes** (alloenzymes) — variant forms of an enzyme that differ **structurally but not functionally**, coded by different alleles **at the same locus**.
- **Isozymes** — enzymes performing the same function but coded by genes at **different loci**.
- Alloenzymes are highly conserved in function across phyla and kingdoms, so phylogeneticists used them as **molecular markers** for evolutionary relationships.
- Because they differ in structure, they can be separated by electrophoresis.
:::

## Losing ground to DNA markers

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p13_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Since the 1960s allozymes played an ongoing role in animal and plant population studies — and then lost the field to DNA markers.

By 2008, microsatellites carried over 80% of published studies and allozymes under 10%.
:::
:::

## Genome sizes compared

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p14_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
The human genome contains **1000×** as many nucleotide pairs as a typical bacterium, **20×** as many genes, and about **10,000×** as much noncoding DNA.

~98.5% of the human genome is noncoding, against 11% for *E. coli*.
:::
:::

## Genome size and number of genes

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p15_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p16_2.jpg)
:::
:::

## Genome size is not gene number



::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lecture2_files/figure-revealjs/genome-plot-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::



Ten thousand-fold more DNA, the same order of magnitude of genes.

# PCR

## DNA replication — the reason PCR works

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- DNA polymerases copy each of the two strands independently, always **5′ → 3′**.
- The strands must be unwound at a **replication fork**.
- Polymerases **cannot initiate synthesis without a primer** — in cells, a short RNA stretch laid down by a primase.

![](/assets/lecture2/p18_3.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p18_2.jpg)
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Supply that primer yourself, from both sides, and you have PCR.
:::

## What a PCR reaction needs

::: {.incremental}
1. **Template DNA** — contains the target region the primers bind and the polymerase copies.
2. **Primers** — short single-stranded DNA, usually **18–30 nt**, complementary to the sequences flanking the target. Forward primer binds the 5′ end of the target; reverse primer binds the 3′ end of the complementary strand.
3. **DNA polymerase** — usually **Taq**, from *Thermus aquaticus*: heat-stable, so it survives the denaturation steps.
4. **dNTPs** — dATP, dTTP, dCTP, dGTP: the building blocks.
5. **Buffer and Mg²⁺** — the cofactor the polymerase cannot work without.
:::

## What a PCR reaction needs

**8. Thermocycler** — precisely controls the temperature changes, cycling through three steps:

| Step | Temperature | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Denaturation | 94–98 °C | double-stranded DNA separates into single strands |
| Annealing | 50–65 °C | primers bind their complementary sequences |
| Extension | ~72 °C | polymerase adds dNTPs to the primed 3′ ends |

**9. Additives (optional)** — DMSO, glycerol, or betaine help with **GC-rich** templates and secondary structure, improving efficiency and specificity under difficult conditions.

## One cycle, drawn out

![](/assets/lecture2/p20_2.jpg){height="240px"}



::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lecture2_files/figure-revealjs/cycler-profile-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::



## Melting temperature (Tm)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p21_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- The temperature at which **50% of the DNA is denatured**.
- G–C pairs have **three** hydrogen bonds; A–T pairs only **two**.
- Matters for **primers** (PCR) and for **probes** (hybridisation).

![](/assets/lecture2/p21_3.jpg)

Rule of thumb: set the annealing temperature **Ta ≈ Tm − 3…5 °C**.
:::
:::

## Primer arithmetic



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
primers <- c(`16S-27F`  = "AGAGTTTGATCCTGGCTCAG",
             `16S-1492R`= "TACGGCTACCTTGTTACGACTT",
             `ITS1`     = "TCCGTAGGTGAACCTGCGG")

tibble::tibble(
  primer = names(primers),
  length = nchar(primers),
  gc     = sapply(primers, gc_pct),
  tm_wallace = sapply(primers, tm_wallace),   # 2(A+T) + 4(G+C)
  tm_gc      = sapply(primers, tm_gc),        # 64.9 + 41(GC - 16.4)/length
  ta_suggested = sapply(primers, tm_gc) - 5
) |> knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|primer    | length|   gc| tm_wallace| tm_gc| ta_suggested|
|:---------|------:|----:|----------:|-----:|------------:|
|16S-27F   |     20| 50.0|         60|  51.8|         46.8|
|16S-1492R |     22| 45.5|         64|  53.0|         48.0|
|ITS1      |     19| 63.2|         62|  55.4|         50.4|


:::
:::



Two rules of thumb, two answers — which is why every new primer pair still needs a **gradient PCR**.

## PCR is exponential

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p22_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p22_3.jpg)



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tibble::tibble(cycle = c(10, 20, 30, 40),
               copies = 2^c(10, 20, 30, 40)) |>
  knitr::kable(format.args = list(big.mark = " "))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


| cycle|       copies|
|-----:|------------:|
|    10| 1.024000e+03|
|    20| 1.048576e+06|
|    30| 1.073742e+09|
|    40| 1.099512e+12|


:::
:::



2⁴⁰ ≈ **10¹²** copies — in theory. In practice reagents run out and the curve plateaus.
:::
:::

## Evolution of thermal cyclers

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p23_2.jpg)

An early PCR machine: three water baths.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p23_3.jpg)

1987 — the first commercial thermal cycler, the TC1.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p23_4.jpg)

A lab-on-chip cassette for PCR.
:::
:::

## qPCR

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p24_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Quantitative PCR** measures DNA *during* amplification.

A DNA dye (e.g. SYBR Green) or a sequence-specific probe is added and **fluorescence is measured every cycle**.

![](/assets/lecture2/p24_3.jpg)

The cycle at which signal crosses the threshold (Cq) is proportional to the log of starting template.
:::
:::

## RT-qPCR

![](/assets/lecture2/p25_2.jpg)

**Quantitative reverse transcription PCR** is used when the starting material is **RNA**: reverse transcriptase makes cDNA first, and the qPCR runs on that.

::: {.callout-note}
"RT" is reverse transcription, not real time. A real-time PCR from DNA is qPCR; from RNA it is RT-qPCR.
:::

## qPCR: multiplexing

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p26_2.jpg)

![](/assets/lecture2/p26_3.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p26_4.jpg)

Combining different **probes and fluorophores**, with different **emission filters and detectors**, lets several targets be quantified in one well.
:::
:::

## Droplet digital PCR (ddPCR)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p27_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
The reaction is split into ~20,000 **droplets**, each an independent nanoreactor. After endpoint PCR, droplets are counted as positive or negative and the starting concentration follows from the **Poisson distribution** — no standard curve.

Right now: considerably **more expensive** than qPCR.
:::
:::

## ddPCR: multiplexing

![](/assets/lecture2/p28_2.jpg)

Two targets, two dyes (FAM and HEX), read as **2D amplitude clusters** — each droplet is assigned to one of four classes.

# Sanger sequencing

## Sanger sequencing (first generation)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p29_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p29_3.jpg)

**"Terminator" nucleotides**: a ddNTP has no 3′-OH, so the chain stops the moment one is incorporated. A population of chains of every possible length is the result.
:::
:::

## Capillary electrophoresis

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p30_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Capillary gel electrophoresis with a **different fluorescent dye linked to each terminator nucleotide**.

One capillary, one laser, one detector — and the four-colour trace we still read today.
:::
:::

## Decoding the gel

Four lanes, one per terminator. Read the ladder from the **bottom** (shortest fragment) upwards — that gives the newly synthesised strand 5′ → 3′:

> Your sequence: **5′-TCGAATGTCAGG-3′**
>
> Template sequence: **3′-AGCTTACAGTCC-5′**

::: {.callout-tip}
The gel gives you the *synthesised* strand. The template is its reverse complement — a step people routinely forget under exam conditions.
:::

## Decode this gel

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p32_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```
ddATP  -
ddTTP  -
ddGTP  -
ddCTP  -
```

Write out the sequence 5′ → 3′, then give the template strand.
:::
:::

# Fragment length polymorphisms

## Restriction nucleases

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p34_2.jpg){height="330px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p34_3.jpg){height="330px"}
:::
:::

Enzymes that cut the double helix at sites defined by the **local nucleotide sequence**. *Hpa*I leaves **blunt** ends; *Eco*RI, *Hin*dIII, and *Pst*I cut in a staggered way, leaving **cohesive** ends. Because the recognition site is only **4–6 bp**, any given DNA yields a consistent set of fragments.

## RFLP — restriction fragment length polymorphism

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p35_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Uses the properties of restriction nucleases; requires **separation and sizing of fragments by electrophoresis**.
- Mutations **destroy or create** cutting sites — that is the polymorphism.
- RFLP can start from:
  1. total DNA extracted from samples;
  2. specific sequences first amplified by PCR.
:::
:::

## PCR-RFLP

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p36_2.jpg){height="380px"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
Amplifying first and digesting afterwards adds:

- **sensitivity** — tiny amounts of starting material suffice;
- **simplicity** — no blotting, no probes, no radioactivity.

A single restriction digest of a PCR product remains one of the cheapest species-diagnostic assays available.
:::
:::

## AFLP — amplified fragment length polymorphism

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p37_2.jpg){height="400px"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
Requires **no sequence information** from the study organism.

1. Digest sample DNA with **two restriction enzymes** giving different overlapping sticky ends.
2. Ligate double-stranded **linkers** with compatible sticky ends.
3. PCR with primers matching the linker sequences plus **1–3 arbitrary selective nucleotides** at the 3′ end.

The whole procedure is a selection in which a small, essentially random proportion of the starting DNA is amplified.
:::
:::

## RAPD — random amplification of polymorphic DNA

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p38_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
A PCR in which the amplified segments are **random**: several arbitrary short primers (**8–12 nt**) are run against a large template of genomic DNA, in the hope that fragments amplify.

Resolving the pattern gives a semi-unique profile.

::: {.callout-warning}
Dominant, and notoriously sensitive to template quality and cycler model — reproducibility between laboratories is the weak point.
:::
:::
:::

## Microsatellite markers

::: {.incremental}
- **Microsatellites** (1–10 nt motifs) and **minisatellites** (>10 nt) are subcategories of **tandem repeats**, which together with interspersed repeats make up the genome's repetitive fraction.
- They matter because they are **unstable**: mutation rates of 10⁻³–10⁻⁶ per cell generation, up to ten orders of magnitude above point mutations.
- SSR, STR, SSLP — the same thing under different names — occur in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, especially in eukaryotic euchromatin, in coding and noncoding, nuclear and organellar DNA.
- They are **not randomly distributed** along the genome.
- Mutations that escape mismatch repair create new alleles, so an SSR locus carries many alleles — making it **more informative than a SNP**.
:::

## Microsatellite markers

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p40_2.jpg)

![](/assets/lecture2/p40_3.jpg){height="240px"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
For more than a decade microsatellite loci were the **marker of choice**.

Traditionally, alleles at one locus were:

- **PCR amplified** with locus-specific primers in the flanking regions;
- **sized by electrophoresis** — the allele *is* the length.
:::
:::

## Replication slippage

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p41_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Replication slippage** is the mutational mechanism behind STRs: the nascent strand dissociates and re-anneals out of register, giving **contraction** or **expansion** by whole repeat units.

The high mutation rate is exactly why many microsatellite loci show **high heterozygosity** — and why they make useful markers.
:::
:::

## ISSR — inter-simple sequence repeats

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p42_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Highly polymorphic, relatively easy to develop, and **inexpensive**.
- A PCR-based system using microsatellite loci across the genome — it amplifies the variation found **between two proximate microsatellite loci** with the same repeat.
- **No sequence information** needed for the study species.
- Weaknesses: poor reproducibility and time-consuming data analysis.
:::
:::

## RADseq — where this is all heading

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/lecture2/p43_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
**Restriction-site associated DNA sequencing** keeps the restriction enzyme but replaces the gel with a sequencer: digest, size-select, sequence the fragments flanking each cut site, and call SNPs across thousands of loci at once.

The logic of RFLP, with the throughput of NGS — which is Lecture 3.
:::
:::

## Choosing a marker

| Marker | Sequence info needed | Dominance | Loci | Main weakness |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Allozymes | no | codominant | tens | sees only charge-changing variation |
| RFLP | some | codominant | few | needs a lot of clean DNA |
| RAPD | no | dominant | many | reproducibility |
| AFLP | no | dominant | hundreds | dominant, complex profiles |
| Microsatellites | yes (flanks) | codominant | tens | development cost, homoplasy |
| SNP / RADseq | no (with RADseq) | codominant | thousands | computation, cost per sample |

## Check yourself

<details>
<summary>Why does agarose separate large molecules better than polyacrylamide?</summary>

Its pore size is much larger, so molecules above ~200 kDa (or above a few kb of DNA) still migrate instead of being trapped at the well.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why must Ta be set below Tm?</summary>

At Tm half the duplex is melted; primers need a temperature where they stay annealed long enough for the polymerase to extend them. Too far below and they anneal to near-matches, giving non-specific product.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why are AFLP and RAPD dominant, but microsatellites codominant?</summary>

AFLP and RAPD score presence or absence of a band, so a heterozygote looks like a dominant homozygote. A microsatellite locus is amplified with locus-specific primers and each allele has its own length, so both alleles are visible.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why does ddPCR not need a standard curve?</summary>

It counts positive and negative droplets at endpoint and converts that fraction to a concentration through the Poisson distribution — an absolute measurement rather than a relative one.

</details>

## Thank you

::: {.callout-important}
peeter.laas@ut.ee · peeter.laas@taltech.ee
:::

**Next lecture:** next-generation sequencing — second generation, third generation, and what they made possible in molecular ecology.

  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
